comments.author: @VagariousTravel-868
comments.text:
率直なフィードバック、ほんとにありがとう。🙏

ちょっとだけ補足させてほしいんだけど、この動画の中でAIで作ったカットはたった1つだけで、長さも4秒間なんだ。なんでかっていうと、その状況をちゃんと伝えられる実際の映像がどうしても見つからなくて、仕方なく視覚的な補助として使った感じ。それ以外のカットは全部実際の映像で、情報も信頼できるソースをもとにしてるよ。

でも、たとえ4秒でもAIが入ってると混乱させたり、信頼を損ねちゃうってのはその通りだと思う。そこはこっちのミスで、ほんとにごめんね。😔

ただ、チームのみんなが企画考えて、脚本書いて、撮影して、編集して……って一生懸命やってきたのが、たった1つの短いカットだけで判断されちゃうのは、やっぱりちょっと悲しい気持ちもあるんだよね。

そもそもこの動画の目的は、日本の地震対策技術を伝えることであって、むしろ日本が地震を乗り越えてきたすごさを称えて、そこから人類が学べる教訓を残したいっていう思いで作ってるんだ。全部、ポジティブなこと、社会や世界にとって良いことを届けたいっていう気持ちからやってる。そこだけはわかってほしいな。

この意見はすごく真剣に受け止めてる。これからはもっと慎重にするし、実際の映像と確かな情報を優先するようにする。それから、どうしてもAIを使わなきゃいけない時は、誤解されないようにちゃんとその旨を表示するようにするね。

指摘してくれて、本当にありがとう。こういうのが届けられる側としてすごく成長させてもらえるよ。❤

comments.author: @VagariousTravel-868
comments.text:
イオンモール熊本の崩壊は地震が原因ではない」という声があります。では、ちょっとお聞きしたいのですが、地震がガス漏れを引き起こし、そのガスが爆発してイオンモールが崩壊したとしたら、原因は何ですか？

皆さんの論理でいくと、こうなります。
地震 → ガス漏れ → ガス爆発 → 建物崩壊 → 下敷きになる → 呼吸ができなくなる → 死亡。

では、この場合の死因は「呼吸ができなくなったこと」なのか、それとも「地震」なのか？

私は、直接のきっかけは地震にあると考えます。もちろん、爆発が直接の死因であることは事実です。しかし、その爆発を引き起こしたのは地震です。原因を「爆発」だけに限定してしまうと、同じことが今後も繰り返されるリスクを見逃してしまうのではないでしょうか。

replies.author: @VagariousTravel-868
replies.text:
Thanks for the honest feedback. 🙏

This video is over an hour long, and most of it is based on real footage and thorough research.
Out of that, I only used AI for 4 seconds. The reason is that for that specific scene, I simply couldn't find any actual footage, so I had to use it as a visual aid.

I totally get why those 4 seconds might bother you. But it's a bit disheartening that hours of work on ideas, scripting, editing, and the whole team's effort get judged based on just a 4-second AI clip.

This video was made to share the brilliance of Japan's earthquake-resistant technology. Not to end earthquakes as just tragedies—but to show what we can learn from them and how we've applied those lessons.

I hope you don't judge the whole thing by those 4 seconds. If you have time, please watch the full video. I'd love to hear your thoughts after that.

Thanks for pointing it out. I'll keep doing my best to share what matters, honestly and sincerely. 🙏

replies.author: @VagariousTravel-868
replies.text:
ご指摘ありがとうございます。イオンモール熊本の爆発が事実である一方、地割れや火災がなかった点については、その通りだと思います。

当方の動画では、地震の規模感や被害の全体像を伝えるために複数の実写映像を編集して使用しておりますが、AI生成の映像を1カ所のみ使用しております（実写映像が見つからなかったため）。その際、視覚的な補助として使用したことが、結果として誤解を招く形になったかもしれません。

いただいたご意見を真摯に受け止め、今後の制作ではより正確な表現と映像の整合性に努めてまいります。

comments.author: @VagariousTravel-868
comments.text:
Thanks for the honest feedback – I really appreciate it. 🙏

Just to clarify: throughout this entire video, we used exactly ONE AI-generated shot, lasting only 4 seconds. The reason is simple – we couldn't find any real footage that clearly depicted that specific situation, so we used it as a temporary visual aid to help get the point across. Every other shot in the video is real footage, and all the information comes from credible sources.

That said, I completely agree that even 4 seconds of AI can cause confusion and hurt trust. That's on us, and I sincerely apologize. 😔

What stings a little is seeing the hard work our entire team put into the concept, scripting, staging, and editing get judged solely on that one brief moment. We genuinely pour our hearts into delivering valuable, truthful content for our viewers.

Going forward, I'm taking this seriously. We'll be much more careful, prioritize real footage and verified information, and clearly label any AI-generated content if we absolutely have to use it – so there's zero room for misunderstanding.

Thanks again for calling this out. It truly helps us get better. ❤️

comments.text: This was such an eye-opening look at Japanese engineering! 🇯🇵 Truly inspiring how they turn tragedy into such resilient innovation.

replies.author: @VagariousTravel-868

comments.author: @OnGod-p7e
comments.text: Japan is on another level when it comes to earthquake engineering. 🇯🇵 The fact that so many massive structures can withstand powerful quakes is honestly incredible. Which Japanese megastructure impressed you the most in this documentary? I'd love to hear everyone's thoughts.

replies.author: @VagariousTravel-868
replies.text: For me, it's the Tokyo Skytree. The fact that it uses a central pillar—basically a modern shinbashira—to sway during quakes is brilliant. It's 634 meters of ancient wisdom wrapped in modern tech. But honestly, the whole city of Tokyo acts like one giant megastructure, constantly being retrofitted and upgraded.

comments.author: @JFCamargo-y5d5u
comments.text: The greatest legacy of Japan's earthquake engineering isn't just stronger buildings—it's the knowledge that helps make communities around the world safer. That's a lesson worth sharing. 🌏🇯🇵🏗

comments.author: @ZviMargaliot
comments.text: Every major earthquake leaves behind valuable lessons. Japan's ability to transform those lessons into safer engineering is what makes these megastructures truly remarkable.

comments.author: @danielyoon-y6b6c
comments.text: Living in one of the world's most active seismic regions has made Japan a global leader in earthquake resilience. This documentary beautifully explores how innovation and experience continue to shape safer cities.

replies.author: @VagariousTravel-868
replies.text: Well said. Japan turned a difficult geography into a living classroom. Every earthquake adds a new chapter to the rulebook. It's not just about surviving—it's about learning and coming back stronger. What part of that learning process do you think has had the biggest impact on how cities are built?

comments.author: @qwertyaqwertasd-g9g
comments.text: Japan's earthquake engineering isn't just about protecting buildings—it's about protecting lives. The lessons learned here have inspired safer construction around the world, and this documentary tells that story beautifully.

comments.author: @SherritaCarmen
comments.text: The way they retrofit old buildings too. Going back and upgrading everything to modern standards. No building left behind.

replies.author: @VagariousTravel-868
replies.text: Exactly. Japan's been retrofitting old buildings for decades. After the 1995 Kobe quake, they pushed hard to bring older structures up to code. Yokohama even offers subsidies for wooden houses—up to 1.15 million yen per household. They're also retrofitting the National Diet Building with base isolation. No building left behind. That's the real commitment.

comments.text: The fact that they've been perfecting this for decades while the rest of us are still figuring it out is wild.

replies.author: @VagariousTravel-868
replies.text: Right? Japan's been at it since the 1960s, while most countries are still catching up. It's not just technology, it's a whole culture of constant improvement. What part of that system do you think took the longest to develop?
